items.stimulus:
On clear nights the Moon looks as fixed in the sky as any landmark, yet it is drifting away from Earth by roughly 3.8 centimetres each year, about the rate at which fingernails grow. The figure comes from laser ranging: observatories fire pulses of light at reflectors left on the lunar surface by crewed and robotic missions, and time how long the light takes to return.

The cause lies in the tides. The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans, raising two bulges of water, one on the side facing the Moon and one on the opposite side. If Earth did not spin, these bulges would sit directly in line with the Moon. However, Earth rotates once a day while the Moon takes about four weeks to complete an orbit, so the planet's rotation drags the bulges slightly ahead of the line joining the two bodies. Friction between moving water and the sea floor is what produces this lag.

The displaced bulge nearest the Moon exerts a small forward pull on it, giving the Moon extra energy and lifting it into a gradually wider orbit. In return, the Moon's pull on the bulge acts like a brake on Earth's spin. The total amount of rotation in the system, which physicists call angular momentum, must stay constant, so whatever Earth loses, the Moon gains. As a result, days are lengthening, though only by around two thousandths of a second per century.

Evidence for this slowing appears in the geological record. Some fossil corals laid down daily growth bands as well as yearly ones, and specimens roughly 400 million years old suggest that a year then contained about 400 days. Because the length of the year is set by Earth's orbit around the Sun, which tides barely affect, more days per year means that each day was shorter.

The present rate of retreat is not thought to be typical of Earth's history. Models suggest it is unusually high today because the shape and size of the current ocean basins make the tides respond strongly to the Moon's pull. In principle, the process would continue until Earth's day matched the Moon's orbital period, but that would take far longer than the Sun is expected to remain stable.

items.stimulus:
Around 1450 in the German city of Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg combined several existing technologies into a workable printing system: individual metal letters that could be rearranged, an oil-based ink that clung to metal, and a press adapted from those used to squeeze grapes and olives. Within fifty years, printing shops were operating in more than two hundred European towns.

It is tempting to picture this spread as the triumph of an obviously superior idea, but the pattern suggests something more ordinary. Printing was a business, and it required large sums of money up front: type had to be cast, paper bought in bulk and workers paid long before any copies were sold. Printers therefore settled where capital, paper supplies and buyers were concentrated. Commercial centres such as Venice, linked to wide trading networks, became major hubs, while many smaller towns saw a press arrive, struggle and close within a few years.

The workers themselves carried the technique. Craftsmen trained in German workshops travelled south and west, setting up shops in Italy, France and elsewhere, often in partnership with local merchants who supplied the funding.

Nor did print sweep away handwriting overnight. Scribes continued to produce books for wealthy clients who valued decoration and exclusivity, and some early printed books were deliberately designed to resemble manuscripts. Seen this way, the press advanced not as a sudden revolution but as a risky trade that followed the money.

items.stimulus:
Tea comes from the leaves of a single evergreen shrub, Camellia sinensis, which is native to the region where southern China meets South-East Asia. For centuries it was drunk mainly in China, first as a medicine and later as an everyday beverage, before monks and diplomats carried both the plant and the habit to Korea and Japan.

Europe encountered tea much later. Dutch merchants were shipping it home by the early seventeenth century, and it soon became fashionable among wealthy households in several countries. In Britain it was at first an expensive luxury, heavily taxed and often smuggled, but as prices fell over the following century it became a drink for every social class.

The routes by which tea travelled have left traces in language. In most varieties of Chinese the word sounds roughly like 'cha', but in the coastal dialect spoken around the port of Xiamen it is closer to 'te'. Places that received tea overland, or through ports where the 'cha' form was used, tend to call it something like 'chai' or 'chá'; this includes Persian, Russian, Hindi and Portuguese. Countries supplied mainly by Dutch ships, which loaded at ports where 'te' was spoken, adopted forms such as 'tea', 'thé' and 'Tee'.

For a long time China held almost complete control over supply, and European buyers paid for tea largely in silver. Seeking an alternative, the British began growing tea on a large scale in north-eastern India during the nineteenth century, using both imported Chinese plants and a variety found growing locally in Assam. Within a few decades India had become a major exporter, and plantations later spread to Sri Lanka and East Africa.

Today tea is, after water, among the most widely consumed drinks in the world, yet the words used to order it still record the ships and caravans that first delivered it.
items.question: Tea reached Korea before it reached Japan.

Tea comes from the leaves of a single evergreen shrub, Camellia sinensis, which is native to the region where southern China meets South-East Asia. For centuries it was drunk mainly in China, first as a medicine and later as an everyday beverage, before monks and diplomats carried both the plant and the habit to Korea and Japan.

Europe encountered tea much later. Dutch merchants were shipping it home by the early seventeenth century, and it soon became fashionable among wealthy households in several countries. In Britain it was at first an expensive luxury, heavily taxed and often smuggled, but as prices fell over the following century it became a drink for every social class.

The routes by which tea travelled have left traces in language. In most varieties of Chinese the word sounds roughly like 'cha', but in the coastal dialect spoken around the port of Xiamen it is closer to 'te'. Places that received tea overland, or through ports where the 'cha' form was used, tend to call it something like 'chai' or 'chá'; this includes Persian, Russian, Hindi and Portuguese. Countries supplied mainly by Dutch ships, which loaded at ports where 'te' was spoken, adopted forms such as 'tea', 'thé' and 'Tee'.

For a long time China held almost complete control over supply, and European buyers paid for tea largely in silver. Seeking an alternative, the British began growing tea on a large scale in north-eastern India during the nineteenth century, using both imported Chinese plants and a variety found growing locally in Assam. Within a few decades India had become a major exporter, and plantations later spread to Sri Lanka and East Africa.

Today tea is, after water, among the most widely consumed drinks in the world, yet the words used to order it still record the ships and caravans that first delivered it.

items.stimulus:
An empty seat on a departing aircraft is a product that can never be sold again. Airlines know from experience that a share of passengers holding tickets will not turn up, whether because they missed a connection, changed their plans or bought a flexible ticket that can be rebooked at no cost. If a flight with 180 seats sold exactly 180 tickets, it would routinely leave with gaps, and the lost revenue would push fares up for everyone else.

To avoid this, carriers sell more tickets than there are seats. The number is not a guess. Forecasting systems estimate no-show rates using records for the particular route, day of the week, season and mix of fares sold; a morning business route full of refundable tickets may justify far more overbooking than a holiday flight on which most travellers have paid non-refundable fares in advance. The airline then weighs the expected revenue from extra sales against the expected cost of having too many passengers at the gate.

When that happens, the cost can be substantial. Passengers who are refused a seat may be entitled to cash compensation, meals, hotel rooms and rebooking, and the reputational damage from a badly handled case can far exceed these sums. For this reason most airlines first ask for volunteers, offering travel credit or money in exchange for taking a later flight. This approach owes much to an economist who argued in the 1960s that, rather than choosing which passengers to remove, airlines should in effect hold an auction and raise the offer until enough people accept. Those who value their seat least give it up, and those who stay are not inconvenienced.

Critics point out that the practice shifts risk onto travellers who have done nothing wrong, and that compensation rules differ widely between jurisdictions. Supporters reply that, on balance, overbooking keeps planes fuller and average fares lower. Either way, being denied boarding remains rare: on most flights the forecast is accurate enough that every passenger who arrives finds a seat.

items.stimulus:
The idea that a child's position among siblings shapes personality has a long history. Early in the twentieth century the psychiatrist Alfred Adler suggested that eldest children tend to be responsible and conservative, while youngest children are more likely to be indulged. Later writers extended such claims, proposing for example that later-born children are more open to new ideas and more willing to challenge authority.

Many early studies appeared to support these ideas, but they shared a weakness. Most compared people from different families, so that a first-born from one household was set against a later-born from another. Because larger families contain more later-born children, and family size is linked to income, parental education and other circumstances, any difference found might reflect the type of family rather than birth order itself. Studies also often relied on ratings by parents or siblings, who may expect the eldest to be the responsible one and describe them accordingly.

In the last decade or so, researchers have attempted to repeat the classic findings using very large samples and better designs, including comparisons between siblings within the same family. Several of these projects, each involving tens of thousands of participants or more, found that the links between birth order and traits such as sociability, emotional stability or openness were either absent or so small as to be meaningless for any individual. One finding did hold up: first-borns scored slightly higher, on average, on tests of intelligence, although the difference was only a point or two and says little about any particular person.

The story illustrates a wider problem. Results that are intuitive and widely reported can persist long after the evidence has weakened, particularly when the original studies were small and the effects they described were easy to recognise in one's own family.

items.stimulus:
A rechargeable lithium-ion battery works by moving lithium ions back and forth. During charging, ions travel through a liquid electrolyte from the positive electrode, usually a metal oxide, and settle between the layers of a graphite negative electrode; during use they flow back, while electrons pass through the device being powered. In an ideal cell this shuttle could continue indefinitely. In practice, every battery gradually holds less charge, and the reasons are mostly chemical side effects of normal operation.

The most important occurs at the graphite surface. During the first few charges, a thin film forms where the electrolyte meets the electrode. This layer is useful, because it stops the electrolyte breaking down further, but building it consumes some of the lithium, which is then no longer available to carry charge. The film never stops growing entirely, and it thickens faster when the battery is hot.

Physical wear also contributes. Electrode materials swell and shrink slightly as ions enter and leave, and over thousands of cycles this can crack particles, cutting some material off from the circuit. Charging very quickly, or charging in freezing conditions, can cause lithium to be deposited as metal on the graphite surface instead of slipping between its layers; this metal is largely lost to future cycles.

Importantly, ageing does not require use. A battery left in a drawer still loses capacity, and the loss is fastest when it is stored fully charged in a warm place. For this reason, some manufacturers now let users stop charging at around 80 per cent, and recommend storing devices that will not be used for months at roughly half charge.

None of these processes can be eliminated entirely, but together they explain why a phone that once lasted a full day may need recharging by mid-afternoon after a few years.

A rechargeable lithium-ion battery works by moving lithium ions back and forth. During charging, ions travel through a liquid electrolyte from the positive electrode, usually a metal oxide, and settle between the layers of a graphite negative electrode; during use they flow back, while electrons pass through the device being powered. In an ideal cell this shuttle could continue indefinitely. In practice, every battery gradually holds less charge, and the reasons are mostly chemical side effects of normal operation.

items.stimulus:
In a book published in 1974, the American philosopher Robert Nozick asked readers to imagine a machine that could give them any experiences they wanted. Connected to it, a person would float in a sealed tank while the device stimulated the brain directly, producing a flawless impression of composing a symphony, falling in love or climbing a mountain. While plugged in, they would not know that the experiences were artificial. Nozick then asked whether you would connect yourself for life.

The question was aimed at hedonism, the view that pleasure, or pleasant experience, is the only thing that is ultimately good for a person. If that view were correct, the machine should be irresistible, since it offers more pleasure than any real life could. Yet Nozick expected most people to refuse, and he suggested several reasons. People care about genuinely carrying out actions, not just about seeming to themselves to carry them out. They also care about what sort of character they have, whereas someone floating in the tank is not really brave, kind or anything else. And they want their lives to connect with something beyond a world that humans have simply manufactured.

Defenders of hedonism have replied in various ways. Some argue that the reluctance reflects worries the scenario is meant to exclude, such as fear that the machine might break down or distrust of whoever runs it. Others point to a bias in favour of whatever situation one is already in. In later studies, people told that their current life was itself produced by such a machine were often unwilling to disconnect, which suggests that attachment to the familiar, rather than a love of reality, may drive some refusals.

These replies do not settle the matter, but they show why the thought experiment remains useful. Whatever one concludes, it forces a person to say what, beyond feeling good, they think makes a life go well.

items.stimulus:
A new medicine can cost hundreds of millions, or even billions, of dollars to develop, much of it spent on clinical trials that end in failure. Once a drug is approved, however, a competitor could often copy the molecule relatively cheaply. Patents exist to address this imbalance. In most countries a patent gives its holder the exclusive right to make and sell an invention for twenty years from the date the application is filed, in exchange for publishing how the invention works.

For medicines, the protected period is shorter than it sounds. Companies usually file patents early, when a compound first looks promising, and the years of testing that follow eat into the term. Some countries, including Australia, allow a limited extension to make up for part of this delay.

When the patent ends, other manufacturers may sell generic versions. They do not need to repeat the full programme of clinical trials; instead they must show that their product contains the same active ingredient and behaves in the body in essentially the same way as the original. Because their costs are far lower, generics are usually cheaper, and prices for the medicine as a whole tend to fall once several suppliers compete.

Critics argue that some companies stretch their monopoly by patenting minor changes, such as a new tablet coating or dosing schedule, in the hope of delaying competition. Others respond that genuine improvements of this kind can benefit patients and deserve protection. The difficulty lies in telling the two apart.

The underlying tension is unlikely to disappear. With too little protection, companies may stop investing in risky research; with too much, patients and health systems pay high prices for longer than necessary. The task for policymakers is not to choose between innovation and access but to set the rules so that each is weighed against the other.

items.stimulus:
In 1935, around a hundred cane toads were shipped from Hawaii to north Queensland in the hope that they would eat beetles damaging the sugar-cane crop. The plan failed: the adult beetles spent much of their time high on the cane stalks, and their larvae lived underground, out of the toads' reach. The toads, however, thrived. A female can lay tens of thousands of eggs at a time, and in Australia the species faced few of the diseases or competitors that limit it in its native range in the Americas. Over the following decades it spread west across northern Australia and south along the east coast, reaching the Northern Territory and eventually Western Australia.

The main damage comes from the toad's toxin, stored in glands on its shoulders. Native predators that had never encountered such an animal, including some goannas, snakes and the northern quoll, a cat-sized marsupial, often die after attacking one. Local populations of these species have fallen sharply in the years after toads arrive, although some have since partly recovered.

The invasion has also changed the toads themselves. Animals at the leading edge of the spread tend to have longer legs and move further each night than those in long-established areas, probably because the fastest individuals keep arriving first and breeding with one another. As a result, the front advanced more quickly in later decades than it did at first.

Since eradication across the continent is now regarded as unrealistic, recent efforts focus on reducing harm. In one approach, predators are offered small pieces of toad meat treated with a substance that causes nausea but no lasting harm, teaching them to avoid toads before the main wave arrives. Some native snakes appear to be adapting without help, with populations in toad-affected areas showing features that make them less likely to eat a toad large enough to kill them.

The cane toad is often cited as a warning about introducing one species to solve a problem caused by another. Its story suggests something further: once an invader is established, the most useful question may be not how to remove it but how to help native wildlife live alongside it.

items.stimulus:
A true fresco is painted onto fresh, damp lime plaster. As the plaster dries, a chemical reaction with carbon dioxide in the air locks the pigment into the surface, which is why such paintings can survive for centuries. Artists often added final details after the plaster had dried, however, using paint mixed with a binder such as glue or egg. These later touches sit on top of the wall rather than within it and are far more easily damaged.

Over time frescoes collect soot from candles and lamps, dust, salts carried by damp, and layers of glue or varnish applied by earlier restorers to brighten faded colours. Removing this material can transform a painting, but it raises a difficult question: how can a restorer be sure that what is being removed is grime rather than something the artist intended?

The most famous dispute concerned the cleaning of the Sistine Chapel frescoes, including Michelangelo's ceiling, carried out between 1980 and 1994. When the work revealed strikingly bright colours, some critics argued that the restorers had stripped away a final layer of shading that Michelangelo had added to dry plaster, leaving the figures flatter than he meant them to be. The restoration team replied that careful analysis showed the darker layers to be mainly smoke deposits and later additions, and that the vivid palette was consistent with other works of the period.

The debate has never been fully resolved, partly because no one can now inspect the surface as it was before cleaning. It did, however, encourage practices that are widely accepted today: recording each stage in detail, testing small areas before larger ones, preferring treatments that can be reversed, and doing as little as is necessary. Restorers increasingly see their role as stabilising a work and slowing its decay rather than returning it to an imagined original state.

items.stimulus:
A true fresco is painted onto fresh, damp lime plaster. As the plaster dries, a chemical reaction with carbon dioxide in the air locks the pigment into the surface, which is why such paintings can survive for centuries. Artists often added final details after the plaster had dried, however, using paint mixed with a binder such as glue or egg. These later touches sit on top of the wall rather than within it and are far more easily damaged.

Over time frescoes collect soot from candles and lamps, dust, salts carried by damp, and layers of glue or varnish applied by earlier restorers to brighten faded colours. Removing this material can transform a painting, but it raises a difficult question: how can a restorer be sure that what is being removed is grime rather than something the artist intended?

The most famous dispute concerned the cleaning of the Sistine Chapel frescoes, including Michelangelo's ceiling, carried out between 1980 and 1994. When the work revealed strikingly bright colours, some critics argued that the restorers had stripped away a final layer of shading that Michelangelo had added to dry plaster, leaving the figures flatter than he meant them to be. The restoration team replied that careful analysis showed the darker layers to be mainly smoke deposits and later additions, and that the vivid palette was consistent with other works of the period.

The debate has never been fully resolved, partly because no one can now inspect the surface as it was before cleaning. It did, however, encourage practices that are widely accepted today: recording each stage in detail, testing small areas before larger ones, preferring treatments that can be reversed, and doing as little as is necessary. Restorers increasingly see their role as stabilising a work and slowing its decay rather than returning it to an imagined original state.

items.question: Leila's final course mark is a weighted average: quizzes 20%, project 30% and final exam 50%. Her quiz component is the mean of her four quiz marks, which were 84, 92, 88 and 96. She scored 64 for the project and 50 in the final exam. All marks are out of 100. What is her final course mark?
items.explanation_ko: 1) 퀴즈 평균: (84 + 92 + 88 + 96) ÷ 4 = 90. 2) 가중 점수: 90 × 0.2 = 18, 64 × 0.3 = 19.2, 50 × 0.5 = 25. 3) 계산기: 18 + 19.2 + 25 = 62.2. 오답: B 65.0은 프로젝트와 시험의 가중치(30%, 50%)를 바꿔 넣은 값, C 68.0은 세 구성요소를 가중치 없이 평균한 값((90 + 64 + 50) ÷ 3), D 74.2는 퀴즈와 시험의 가중치를 바꾼 값, E 79.0은 점수 6개(퀴즈 4개, 프로젝트, 시험)를 단순 평균한 값이다. 가장 비중이 큰 시험 점수가 가장 낮으므로 정답이 가장 작다. → 정답 A

Mei recognises the name of the ward printed at the top but does not know who the pages belong to. Her next placement day is in two days' time. How appropriate are each of the following responses by Mei in this situation?
items.question: Keep the pages secure at home and hand them to the ward manager at her next placement day, in two days.

options.text: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do

items.explanation_ko: 1) 문서를 회수해 안전하게 보관하고 병동 관리자에게 돌려주므로 추가 노출을 막고 병원이 사고를 알게 된다. 그래서 C 이하가 아니다. 2) 그러나 '이틀 뒤(in two days)'까지 알리지 않으면 병원이 정보 유출 사고를 늦게 파악하고, 문서를 잃어버린 직원도 그동안 모른다. 당일 병동에 전화하는 등 더 빨리 알리는 것이 이상적이다. 3) 안전하지만 지연이 있으므로 A가 아니라 B다. → 정답 B (적절하지만 이상적이지 않음)

Theo wrote the message on a scrap of paper and then forgot about it. At 3 pm he finds the paper in his pocket and hears that the team is planning Mr Lindqvist's discharge later today. How appropriate are each of the following responses by Theo in this situation?
items.question: Immediately tell the nurse in charge and the doctor responsible about the message, explaining that he forgot to pass it on.

options.text: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do

items.explanation_ko: 1) 퇴원이 오늘 계획되어 있으므로 보호자의 요청이 바로 전달되어야 안전한 퇴원 준비가 가능하다. 즉시 알리는 것은 환자 안전을 지킨다. 2) '전달을 잊었다(he forgot)'고 밝히는 것은 자신의 실수를 적절한 사람에게 바로 공개하는 정직성(honesty)의 원칙에 맞다. 3) 안전과 정직 두 측면을 모두 해결하므로 B로 낮출 이유가 없다. → 정답 A (매우 적절함)
